extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists/short-story authors) exploring nonlinear structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using multiple timelines (flashbacks, in medias res, intercutting) in fiction to dramatize backstory, control pacing, and deepen theme/character without killing forward momentum or confusing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize backstory in scene rather than infodump
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple timelines to dramatize back story, telling it in scene instead of having a big info dump.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave past scenes back and forth with present action so the past is as compelling as the present. Example: Shadow of the Wind—when the protagonist discovers something, the narrative jumps back to show that epiphany happening rather than simply reporting it. Anti-pattern: long expository blocks that read like history lessons rather than scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use timelines to feed information and control pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the reader experiences everything linearly; multiple timelines are a tool for when and how you feed them information and for controlling pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan which timeline supplies which piece of information and when, using jumps to maintain suspense or accelerate/slow rhythm. Example: alternating chapters in Inheritance of Orquidea Divina prevent revealing key facts too early. Scoring note: effective use results in well-timed reveals; poor use spoils or confuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure each timeline jump carries tension and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever you jump to another timeline, that sequence should carry its own tension and story value, not merely pause the main plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a flashback feels like a digression or an info-dump, it kills momentum. Make past scenes serve character or plot development in a compelling way. Anti-pattern: flashbacks that make readers want to 'go get a sandwich.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make flashbacks answer an immediately raised question
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful flashback should usually be an answer to a question that just landed on the reader, rather than creating new unanswered questions or stalling progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard's rule of thumb: flashbacks should resolve or illuminate something the reader/frontline character has just encountered. Avoid flashbacks that merely introduce tangential mysteries or delay answers unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the past timeline to legitimize hard-to-believe elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing a surprising or hard-to-buy element in a past timeline can make it feel more believable simply by establishing history and precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition and the existence of a precedent (e.g., 'this happened 122 years ago') helps readers suspend disbelief. Use past events as corroboration for present weirdness or worldbuilding. Example: using historical mentions/legends to sell magic or unusual plot points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving away the ending or key revelations prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure timeline alternation so readers discover things with characters and so the past does not reveal outcomes before they matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the sequence of reveals across timelines so tension and mystery remain intact; alternating chapters can let readers discover past events in step with present investigation. Anti-pattern: presenting past material that spoils the stakes or solutions for present characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat parallel timelines as separate narrative curves and synchronize climaxes where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Each timeline can have its own narrative arc; intercutting them can increase tension and emotional investment, especially if their climaxes align.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan each timeline's dramatic curve so intercutting raises stakes (example: Julie & Julia). Use intercutting to escalate momentum by timing rising action and payoffs to complement each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple timelines to compare and contrast and deepen theme/character
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching between times can highlight continuities or contrasts (character motivations, cultural change, recurring patterns) that deepen theme and characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Firebird contrasts eras and shows what doesn't change; When I Wake Up uses simultaneous colored timelines to explore choices. Use contrasts intentionally to reveal insight rather than as a mere gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build reader trust and set nonlinearity rules early
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers must learn how and why you will jump in time; establish the pattern or rules of your structure early so later jumps feel justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you establish up front that the story will hop around (or label scenes), readers will accept it. V. E. Schwab's Vicious builds trust by setting reader expectations early; lack of such scaffolding risks annoyance or confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal timeline shifts clearly (labels, date headers, color, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit signals—time stamps, phrases like 'ten years before', consistent headers, or visual cues—to help readers track which timeline they are in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vicious often prefixed scenes like 'ten years before'; picture books may use color-coding. Good signaling reduces cognitive load and prevents disorientation when you hop frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate timeline architecture for your story
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you need a single timeline with flashbacks, forked/alternate timelines, or interacting timelines (where events across timelines affect each other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard distinguishes single timeline pointers (present/flashback) from true forked timelines (alternate realities) and interacting timelines (e.g., Frequency, where timelines can communicate). Each has different narrative consequences—pick the one that fits your premise and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use multiple timelines gratuitously—ensure they enhance the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Only add a second timeline if it enhances character insight, motivation, mystery depth, or thematic complexity in ways a single timeline would not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework recommendation: try adding a second timeline to your WIP to see if it enhances character motivation or illuminates plot points. If it merely complicates reading without adding depth, remove it.
